title: Three Red Panda Cubs Are the Star of This Panda Party
summary:
Happy International Red Panda Day! At the Smithsonian's National Zoo, there are three tiny reasons to celebrate.

Three red panda cubs were born this summer at the zoo's campus in Front Royal, Virginia. On May 29, a mom named Sequoia and dad Mow Mow had twins — one girl, one boy. On June 11, a mom named Keahi had a single girl.

All three are doing well. They've spent the summer in nest boxes, drinking milk and sleeping. They're starting to move around more, and their personalities are showing.

"The singleton... is definitely feisty and huff-quacks at us every chance she gets," said Jessica Kordell, an assistant curator. "The twins are a bit more quiet and shy."

Red pandas are endangered. Fewer than 10,000 live in the wild, in the treetops of Nepal, India, Bhutan, Myanmar, and China. They eat mostly bamboo — about two to four pounds a day — but can digest only about 24 percent of it. That's why they eat so much!

Their red fur helps them blend in with reddish lichen growing on trees. Their black bellies fade into shadows.

Why does this matter? These cubs pass their parents' genes to the next generation. That helps keep the species going.
why_it_matters: Learning about endangered animals like red pandas shows kids how zoos and people can help: when a species' forest home is in danger, every new cub — and every protected tree — makes a difference.

background_read: The Smithsonian's National Zoo (a famous zoo in Washington, D.C., run by the Smithsonian, a big U.S. museum and science group) runs programs to breed red pandas and other rare animals.
Red pandas (small, reddish animals with bushy tails that live in the mountain forests of Asia — they are not actually pandas) spend much of their time in trees.
Wild red pandas are endangered mostly because the forests they live in are being cut down, so zoo births help keep the species from disappearing.
Article_Structure: WHO: Three red panda cubs at the Smithsonian's National Zoo — twins (a girl and a boy) born May 29 to mom Sequoia and dad Mow Mow, and a single girl born June 11 to mom Keahi.
WHAT: The cubs spent the summer in nest boxes drinking milk and sleeping; now they are moving around more and showing their personalities — one feisty, the twins quieter and shy.
WHERE: The zoo's campus in Front Royal, Virginia; in the wild, red pandas live in the treetops of Nepal, India, Bhutan, Myanmar, and China.
WHY: The cubs pass their parents' genes to the next generation, which helps keep the endangered species going.

perspectives.description: They are celebrating three healthy cubs and happily describe each one's personality, from the feisty single girl to the quiet twins.
They are glad the zoo is breeding red pandas, but point out that the real problem is the loss of forests where wild red pandas live.
They see zoo births as one tool for saving a species. The final goal is a healthy wild population, not just cubs in a zoo.
